question: What else can cause dry eye?
answer:
Other causes of dry eye include:
- Medicines. Dry eye can be a side effect of some medicines that treat conditions like colds and allergies, depression, and high blood pressure [nei_039_chunk_02].
- Health problems. Some health problems — including diabetes, thyroid problems, and autoimmune disorders like lupus or Sjögren syndrome — can cause dry eye [nei_039_chunk_02].
- Laser eye surgery. After some types of laser surgery, your eyes may produce fewer tears [nei_039_chunk_02].
- Windy, smoky, or dry environments. Spending time in these types of places can cause your tears to dry up faster and lead to dry eye [nei_039_chunk_02].
- Looking at screens for long periods of time. You may blink less when looking at computer or tablet screens, which can lead to dry eye [nei_039_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: Something is stuck under my eyelid and I can't blink it out. What should I do?
answer:
If something is stuck under your eyelid and you can't blink it out, please see your eye doctor or go to the emergency room. Don’t try to remove it yourself — you could scratch your cornea [nei_025_chunk_03].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What other health problems can blepharitis cause?
answer:
Blepharitis can lead to other eye problems, including:
- Stye. A stye is a red, painful bump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland [nei_007_chunk_04].
- Chalazion. A chalazion is a hard, painless lump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland [nei_007_chunk_04].
- Dry eye. Oil and flakes can build up in your tear film (a thin layer of tears across the surface of your eye). This can make your eyes feel dry [nei_007_chunk_04].
- Damage to the cornea. In severe cases, blepharitis can hurt your cornea (the clear outer layer at the front of your eye) [nei_007_chunk_04].
- Chronic (long-term) red eye. Blepharitis can make the white part of your eye look red all the time [nei_007_chunk_04].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: I see spots and my vision is sometimes fuzzy. What could it be?
answer:
Please get an eye exam to check for AMD, diabetic retinopathy, or floaters, as these can cause symptoms like spots and blurry vision [nei_003_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What causes macular edema?
answer:
Macular edema happens when blood vessels leak into a part of the retina called the macula, causing it to swell [nei_005_chunk_02]. The most common cause is diabetic retinopathy, an eye condition that causes vision loss in people with diabetes [nei_005_chunk_02]. Other causes can include:
- Certain medicines, like those used to treat glaucoma [nei_005_chunk_04].
- Non-diabetic retinal conditions [nei_005_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What is retinal detachment?
answer:
Retinal detachment happens when your retina (a light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of your eye) is pulled away from its normal position [nei_050_chunk_01]. It can be caused by a tear or break in the retina, scar tissue pulling on the retina, or fluid buildup behind the retina [nei_050_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What is dry eye?
answer:
Dry eye happens when your eyes don’t make enough tears to stay wet, or when your tears don’t work correctly [nei_006_chunk_01]. This can make your eyes feel uncomfortable, and in some cases it can also cause vision problems [nei_006_chunk_01]. Symptoms can include burning, dry or scratchy feeling, blurry vision, red eyes, and sensitivity to light [nei_006_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: How is pink eye treated?
answer:
Most cases of pink eye get better on their own [nei_046_chunk_01]. You can use over-the-counter artificial tears to help your eyes feel less dry [nei_046_chunk_01].

If your pink eye is caused by an infection, it can be contagious [nei_046_chunk_01]. To prevent spreading:
- Don’t share towels, bed sheets, or makeup
- Throw out tissues after wiping your eyes
- Wash your hands frequently [nei_046_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What symptoms can macular edema cause?
answer:
Macular edema can cause symptoms such as blurry or wavy vision, and vision that gets worse over time [nei_005_chunk_01]. You may also notice that objects look wavy, especially when you look straight ahead [nei_005_chunk_01]. If you only have macular edema in one eye, it may take longer to notice changes to your vision [nei_005_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: How will my child’s doctor check for amblyopia?
answer:
Your child’s doctor will look for signs of amblyopia as part of a normal vision screening, and all kids ages 3 to 5 need to have their vision checked at least once [nei_022_chunk_04]. Symptoms can be hard to notice, and kids with amblyopia may have poor depth perception, squinting, shutting 1 eye, or tilting their head [nei_022_chunk_02]. Amblyopia is diagnosed through an eye exam [nei_022_chunk_01].

question: What are the symptoms of refractive errors?
answer:
- The most common symptom is blurry vision [nei_009_chunk_01]. Other symptoms include double vision, hazy vision, seeing a glare or halo around bright lights, squinting, headaches, eye strain, and trouble focusing when reading or looking at a computer [nei_009_chunk_02].

- Astigmatism can make far-away and nearby objects look blurry or distorted [nei_009_chunk_01].

- Presbyopia makes it hard for middle-aged and older adults to see things up close [nei_009_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What are the symptoms of cataracts?
answer:
Please see the page: Cataracts — What are the symptoms of cataracts? (updated 2026-08-19) [nei_001_chunk_02].

- You might not have any symptoms at first, when cataracts are mild.
- But as they grow, cataracts can cause changes in your vision. For example:
  - Your vision is cloudy or blurry
  - Colors look faded
  - You can’t see well at night
  - Lamps, sunlight, or headlights seem too bright
  - You see a halo around lights
  - You see double (this sometimes goes away as the cataract gets bigger)
  - You have to change the prescription for your glasses or contact lenses often
- Talk with your eye doctor if you have any of these symptoms — they could also be signs of other eye problems.

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What are the symptoms of floaters?
answer:
Floaters are small dark shapes that float across your vision [nei_015_chunk_01]. They can look like spots, threads, squiggly lines, or even little cobwebs [nei_015_chunk_01]. Most people have floaters that come and go, and they often don’t need treatment [nei_015_chunk_01].

You may notice floaters more when you look at something bright, like white paper or a blue sky [nei_015_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: I suddenly see flashing lights and a shower of floaters in my left eye. What should I do?
answer:
Please get care now, preferably from an eye doctor or emergency room, if you suddenly see flashing lights and a shower of floaters in your left eye. These symptoms can be a sign of a retinal tear or retinal detachment, which can be a medical emergency [nei_015_chunk_03].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What are the symptoms of presbyopia?
answer:
Symptoms of presbyopia include:
- Trouble seeing things up close
- Needing to hold reading materials farther away to focus on them
- Eye strain (when your eyes feel tired or sore)
- Headache [nei_013_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What is uveitis?
answer:
Uveitis is inflammation inside your eye [nei_021_chunk_01]. It usually happens when your immune system is fighting an infection [nei_021_chunk_01]. Sometimes uveitis means your immune system is fighting an eye infection — but it can also happen when your immune system attacks healthy tissue in your eyes [nei_021_chunk_01].

This inflammation can cause symptoms like blurry vision, floaters, eye pain, red eyes, and sensitivity to light [nei_021_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

question: What happens during LASIK surgery?
answer:
During LASIK surgery, a small flap is cut in the cornea and folded back, allowing the laser to reshape the cornea into the correct shape [nei_049_chunk_03]. The flap is then replaced in place. The procedure is performed after an eye exam that uses a scanner to create a detailed image of the cornea [nei_049_chunk_03].

question: How can I prevent cataracts?
answer:
To prevent cataracts, you can take steps to protect your eyes:
- Protect your eyes from the sun. Wear sunglasses and a hat with a brim to block the sun.
- Protect your eyes from injury. While doing activities like using power tools or playing certain sports, wear protective eyewear to protect your eyes from getting accidentally injured.
- Quit smoking. If you’re ready to quit, call 1-800-QUIT-NOW (1-800-784-8669) for free support.
- Make eye-healthy food choices. Eat plenty of healthy foods — like fruits and vegetables, leafy greens, nuts, and whole grains.

question: How often do I need to get a dilated eye exam?
answer:
How often you need to get a dilated eye exam depends on your risk for eye disease [nei_028_chunk_01]. Talk to your doctor about what’s right for you [nei_028_chunk_01].

Get a dilated eye exam every 1 to 2 years if:
- Are over age 60
- Are African American and over age 40
- Have a family history of glaucoma [nei_028_chunk_01].

If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, ask your doctor how often you need an exam [nei_028_chunk_01].

question: Farsightedness and presbyopia are the same thing, right?
answer:
No. Farsightedness (hyperopia) and presbyopia are not the same thing. Farsightedness is a refractive error that makes nearby objects look blurry, and it can be present from birth or early childhood [nei_048_chunk_02].

Presbyopia is an age-related condition that makes it hard to see things up close, and it usually starts after age 45 [nei_013_chunk_02].

question: What is farsightedness?
answer:

question: What can I do to prevent diabetic retinopathy?
answer:
To prevent diabetic retinopathy, it’s important to manage your diabetes effectively. Keeping your blood sugar levels in a healthy range can lower your risk [nei_004_chunk_07]. You can also get a special lab test called an A1C test to check your average blood sugar level over the past 3 months [nei_004_chunk_07].

Having high blood pressure or high cholesterol along with diabetes increases your risk for diabetic retinopathy [nei_004_chunk_07].

question: How do eye doctors check for RP?
